title: Sharp multiserver pricing guarantees and the worst congestion load
shortTitle: A fixed price with a cap: the published guarantees cannot be improved
oneLine: The published worst-case guarantees for a throughput-matched static price with a capacity cap are exact for every number of servers, with an explicit worst congestion load and an exact revenue-congestion curve.
abstract: A simple static price with a capacity cap has published worst-case guarantees for profit, revenue and congestion, and Bergquist and Elmachtoub conjectured that their multiserver bounds cannot be improved. This candidate proves all three sharpness claims for every number of servers and every capacity, with uniform valuations. It finds the offered load that maximises the congestion ratio: an explicit quartic decides between an interior maximiser and critical load, and also decides whether the worst revenue and congestion ratios can be approached together. Its waiting-capacity threshold is asymptotic to 1.7882539728 times the square root of the number of servers. The paper also proves the many-server limit of the maximal ratio, the exact worst-case revenue-congestion frontier, and sharpness of the companion sojourn-time guarantees. With five servers and capacity seven the construction keeps at least 81.85% of optimal revenue and raises occupancy by at most a factor 1.01003, and the congestion figure occurs at a load of about 2.59 rather than 5. These results concern the specified throughput-matched construction, not the best static policy, which stays open. The optimal throughput is a proof device, and the occupancy ratio can hide queues. The frontier and sojourn proofs are elementary with close antecedents. Pacheco (1994) has the same threshold for one server, and the two differ at two servers. This is not a priority claim.

keyResults: Sharpness (Theorem 2.1, Proposition 3.4, proof): the profit, revenue and congestion constants are sharp for every C and N, even for uniform valuations; optimal throughput runs through all of (0,C) in the linear-demand family.
Worst load (Theorem 2.2, proof): an explicit quartic Q_C decides whether the congestion ratio peaks below critical load; the threshold is asymptotic to 1.7882539728√C.
Joint attainability (Corollary 4.1, proof): the worst revenue and congestion ratios can be approached together exactly when d ≥ d_crit(C).
Exact frontier (Theorem 4.3, Proposition 4.2, proof): the load-dependent bounds are tight at every load, giving the whole worst-case revenue-congestion curve.
Many servers and rates (Theorems 6.1, 7.1, Corollary 6.2, proof): limits of the maximal ratio and its maximiser with c√C waiting places, and finite-parameter bounds on the profit deficit.
Sojourn time (Theorem 8.1, proof): the companion sojourn-time constants are sharp and always approached together.

narration:
This is a short audio briefing on a new Evidence Press research candidate: sharp multiserver pricing guarantees and the worst congestion load.

Imagine a service with several servers. It could change its price with every change in demand. Or it could keep one simple fixed price, and cap how many customers it holds. How much does the simple rule lose? In a recent paper, Bergquist and Elmachtoub published worst-case guarantees for a particular fixed-price rule, and they conjectured that those guarantees could not be improved.

This paper proves it, for every number of servers and every capacity. Here is an example. With five servers and room for seven customers, the rule keeps at least 81.85 percent of the best possible revenue, and raises average occupancy by a factor of at most 1.01003. Neither number can be improved.

The paper then goes further. It finds the load at which congestion is worst: here about 2.59, while the revenue figure arises as the load approaches five. An exact formula says when those two worst cases can occur together. The paper also gives the exact trade-off curve between revenue and congestion, and shows that the companion guarantees for time spent in the system cannot be improved either.

Some limits. These results concern one specified construction, not the best fixed price, and that question stays open. The rule uses a quantity called the optimal throughput, which is a proof device: anyone who could compute it could simply set the best price. The occupancy ratio can hide a queue. With one hundred servers and capacity one hundred and twenty, the worst ratio is only 1.033, yet the average queue at full load is about six. The frontier and sojourn proofs are elementary, with close antecedents. Pacheco, in 1994, has the same threshold for one server, but the two differ at two servers. This is not a priority claim.

The proofs are written out, and scripts check the numbers. Review was internal and AI-assisted, with no proof assistant. This remains an unrefereed candidate, released on 4 November 2026. The paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press page.

This briefing uses a synthetic voice, and it is not additional scientific evidence.
